The original public key algorithms used when e.g. HTTPS starts up can in theory be broken by quantum computing, for example by factoring the RSA modulus. According to https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization_records#Records_for_efforts_by_quantum_computers, the largest number so far factored by anything resembling a quantum computer is 291,331 which can easily be factored by traditional means. Researchers and standardizers are working on producing quantum-resistant public key algorithms to replace the current ones.

Once HTTPS has used a public key algorithm at the start of a connection, it uses a private key algorithm, such as AES, for the bulk of the data. There is no obvious way to use quantum computers to attack these productively. The most attractive theories are equivalent to halving the length of the key, and these algorithms have been sized with key length to spare. If we really had to, we could achieve much of what we can achieve with public key systems using only private key systems, at the cost of having to trust a few specialized central computer systems with the entire security of the system. The Kerberos system, in which Microsoft computer systems owned by a single company trust the Domain Controllers operated by that company, is an example of this.

Where only security matters there is an encryption system called the One Time Pad which is theoretically unbreakable, but in practice so inconvenient that most people either don't use it or don't use it securely. Reportedly, this is used by the Washington-Moscow hot line.

The most practical way to subvert the security of an entire computer system is to subvert one of the system operators, or at least somebody who can get close to the system with screwdrivers and so on. Similarly, the best way of securing a computer system is to make sure it is not connected to a network, put it in a locked room, and surround it with armed guards (and leave it switched off :-)).
